title: A Clock on a Track
bigQuestion: How did a running race become eight lanes and eight times?

story.title: A Hand Drops
story.kicker: A hand drops and eight lanes become eight times.
paragraphs: Eight painted lanes curve around an oval. A starter holds a gun or a whistle. When the signal comes, eight bodies become eight times. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
A standard outdoor track is 400 meters around in the inside lane. World Athletics writes many of those technical rules. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
Time is an object here: a stopwatch, later a photo-finish camera. The clock is as much a part of the room as the paint. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
The IHSA crowned its first track and field state champions in 1893, earlier than most of its other sport series. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
story.think: What does a stopwatch remember that the dirt will forget?

lessons.title: Four Hundred Meters
lessons.mainIdea: A standard outdoor running track is 400 meters around in the inside lane.
reading: World Athletics sets the standard outdoor lap at 400 meters in lane one. School tracks in many countries copy that length.
Older American meets used yards. A 440-yard lap is close to 400 meters but is not the same number.
When two schools compare times, they need to know which lap they ran.

words.d: one full trip around the track
the international body that writes many track technical rules

look.prompt: Which number is the standard outdoor lap?

check.q: Who writes many international track rules?

choices: close to 400 meters but not the same

lessons.title: Lanes as Fair Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Staggered starting marks make the outer lanes as long as the inside lane for one lap.
reading: An outer lane is a bigger circle. If every runner started on the same line, the outside runner would run farther.
Staggered starts paint a different mark in each lane so one full lap is the same distance.
The stagger is geometry on the ground. It is a fairness tool written into the marks.

words.d: a marked strip one runner stays in
a starting mark moved forward in outer lanes

look.title: Eight marks
look.text: Look at eight starting marks that step forward as the lanes go out. The finish line is one painted bar.
look.prompt: Why don't the outer-lane marks sit even with lane one?

choices: one lap is the same distance

lessons.title: The Ancient Stadium
lessons.mainIdea: The ancient Olympic Games at Olympia included a sprint in a stadium, a long dirt path.
reading: A stade was a unit of length and a place. Runners raced a straight path, not a modern 400-meter oval.
The traditional date for the first ancient Olympic Games is 776 BCE. That date is a later count, not a stopwatch tape.
Modern ovals and ancient paths are both rooms built so a race can be seen.

words.d: the place in Greece of the ancient Olympic Games
an ancient race path and a unit of length

look.title: A path, not an oval
look.text: Ancient Olympic running at Olympia used a stadium path. The traditional first Games are dated 776 BCE. The modern 400-meter oval is a later room.

lessons.title: The Stopwatch
lessons.mainIdea: A stopwatch turns a race into a number a page can keep.
reading: Before pocket watches were common, races were won by the eye: who reached the mark first.
A stopwatch lets officials write minutes and seconds. Two meets on two days can be compared.
The object on the table is the watch, not a runner's stride.

words.d: a clock that starts and stops to measure a race
the person who writes the time as the meet record

lessons.title: Photo Finish
lessons.mainIdea: Photo-finish cameras later decided close races the eye could not split.
reading: At the tape, two runners can look even. A camera aimed at the finish line records the order.
Photo finish became standard in high-level meets in the twentieth century.
The picture is evidence. It is another kind of paper, made of light.

words.d: a camera record of the exact order at the finish line
the finish line of a race

look.title: Two chests, one line
look.text: Look at two runners leaning. A camera sits beside the line. The official waits for the picture.
look.prompt: Why might the picture be fairer than a shout?

choices: the eye cannot split the race

lessons.title: Starting Blocks
lessons.mainIdea: Starting blocks are a later tool that holds a sprinter's feet at the start.
reading: Older sprinters dug holes in the cinders for their feet. Blocks later gave a standard object.
World Athletics events use blocks in short races. The object belongs at the starting mark.
Blocks are gear. They are not a lesson in how to sprint.

words.d: a frame that holds a sprinter's feet at the start
the old burned-surface tracks where runners dug footholds

look.title: From holes to frames
look.text: Sprinters once dug footholds in cinder tracks. Starting blocks became the standard object at the start of short races.
look.cite: World Athletics starting-block practice; cinder-track histories

lessons.title: IHSA Track, 1893
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first track and field state champions in 1893.
reading: Among IHSA sports, track and field is early. The first champions were named in 1893, seven years before the association's 1900 founding date as now counted, in the lineage of Illinois school meets.
The IHSA history page lists Track and Field at 1893 for the first state champion.
School tracks in Illinois still host that series. The oval is a civic room like the gym.

lessons.title: A School Meet Needs Officials
lessons.mainIdea: A track meet needs starters, timers, and judges as well as runners.
reading: Someone must fire or blow the start. Someone must watch the line. Someone must write the time.
Those jobs are public. A meet without paper is only a practice.
IHSA series rules name how those officials work. The names of the jobs are history of the room.

words.d: the official who gives the start signal
the official who records the time

look.title: Three chairs
look.text: Look at a starter's stand, a timer's watch, and a clipboard at the finish. Three jobs. One race.
look.prompt: What would be missing if one chair were empty?

lessons.title: Comparing Marks Across Towns
lessons.mainIdea: Written times let a school in Cairo and a school in Rockford compare marks.
reading: If both run 400 meters on a marked track, the numbers can sit on one list.
If one school still ran yards and the other ran meters, the list would lie.
Shared length plus shared timing is why track paper travels.

words.d: a recorded time or distance from a meet
the unit of the standard outdoor lap

look.title: One list
look.text: State series and record lists work only when schools use the same measured lap and the same way of writing time.
